This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a $d$-dimensional hypercube governed by the Schrödinger equation. Under the premise that the ground state can be found within a specific class of functions, we establish that the convergence rate of the training algorithm is stochastic. Specifically, when the bias variance is set, we demonstrate the convergence rate is at most $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\log^2(1/\delta)}{N_\text{train}}\right)$ for a confidence level of $1-\delta$. Furthermore, when the bias variance is set, we show the convergence rate is $\mathcal{O}(N_\text{train}^{-2})$ with a high probability. These findings signify the feasibility of two-layer neural networks for solving high-dimensional quantum ground state problems using a limited number of training data points.

Homogenization outcomes for thin films, reduced by dimensional reduction, were derived 
under periodic or almost periodic hypotheses in film mid-plane energies. In this note, 
we discuss thin films, resulting from cross-sections of periodic mediums, with incommensurate 
mid-planes - containing no period other than zero - and demonstrate a generalized 
homogenization outcome via geometric, almost periodic reasoning.

For the time-dependent Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker spacetime, we have derived the non-linear self-interacting Dirac field, solving it for various scenarios and expressing the field in a expanded form for particular limiting cases. Additionally, we have also solved the interacting Dirac equation for a specific Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi spacetime.

In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its efficiency in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the identification of tumor cells within digital histopathology slides. By incorporating histological markers to highlight distinct cell types within the slides, our study involved classifying distinct cell types within individual tumor samples. Our results showed that federated learning produced consistent classifications across various tumor types, even when using diverse sets of trained models. Furthermore, the approach offered several advantages, including the ability to train models across unique datasets from different institutions, each with their own unique training requirements, while also accommodating varying levels of annotation quality. In effect, federated learning provided a reliable platform for model training, despite challenges related to data heterogeneity.

Cavity magnomechanics offers a unique platform for exploring the macroscopic quantum interactions between two-dimensional magnetic materials, mechanical systems and resonant cavities. This system enables researchers to manipulate the macroscopic quantum states of magnons and phonons by exploiting linear and nonlinear interactions between the components. Specifically, the nonlinearity within this system can be harnessed for the quantum state engineering of phonons and magnons through the application of a drive force and strong magnetic field in the anti-PT-symmetric phase. By utilizing techniques such as parametric amplification and magnon-phonon coupling, researchers can achieve a wide range of phonon states and magnonic bound states in magnon-phonon clusters. Furthermore, phascols, which are elusive states combining features of magnons and phonons, can be generated and made to interfere with one another, offering potential applications in quantum information processing.

Recent advancements in reinforcement learning have led to remarkable achievements in the field of robotic locomotion. However, their application is often limited to flat, constrained environments due to the complexity of learning on random terrain. A novel approach combines reinforcement learning with an innovative algorithm called Evolutionary Terrain Generation to enable robust learning on diverse and complex surfaces. The Evolution Terrain Generation algorithm facilitates parallel simulation and evolution of the robot's locomotion by generating and modifying the environment in real-time, resulting in a trained policy that can navigate randomly evolved terrains with ease. Our method's efficacy has been demonstrated by successfully training a 12-degree-of-freedom quadrupedal robot using model-free reinforcement learning, allowing it to traverse random pitched surfaces in both flat and obstacle-filled environments using various locomotion techniques such as walking, bounding, and bounding.

The behavior of supermassive black holes in their intermediate luminosity range
has not been extensively studied, and whether it generates a hot gas outflow is
still a subject of debate.  The high-resolution X-ray observation of NGC 7213
was conducted using the XMM-Newton satellite, and a detailed spectral analysis
was performed.  The results of this study show that it has an estimated
luminosity of approximately $3 \times 10^{43}$ erg/s and exhibits a distinctive
x-ray spectrum.  By comparing theoretical models such as thermal models and
non-thermal models to the observed x-ray data, we found that a hot gas model
with a temperature of around $2.4 \times 10^7$ K, emitting power of around
$2.5 \times 10^{42}$ erg/s, provides the best fit to the observed x-ray data.
Our study supports the notion that the hot gas component is a result of the
heat generated by the intermediate black hole, and its velocity has been
calculated as approximately 570 km/s relative to the black hole based on the
Doppler shift effect, which indicates a high-speed outflow from the black
hole for the first time.  The discovery of a hot gas outflow from a black hole
with a medium mass provides valuable insights for understanding black hole
wind phenomena and the high-speed jet

Closed-loop system performance can decline over time due to plant aging and changes, prompting the need to adjust feedback gains through redesigning the optimal regulator without knowing the original plant model or its original optimal control solution. Reinforcement learning, particularly its two-step version, offers a potential paradigm shift in control design by offering a viable approach to optimizing performance under various plant conditions. However, incorporating a model-based initial tuning step significantly improves its efficiency and adaptability to different plant scenarios. In this research, we develop a hybrid method combining two-step reinforcement learning and an existing approach to adjust the optimal linear regulator, ensuring the optimized solution maintains its original stabilizing properties. Our proposed algorithm only requires multiple samples of the open-loop and closed-loop plant responses along with desired performance criteria to achieve optimal control. Simulations confirm its effectiveness in achieving optimal performance across various plant variations and analyzing the impact of initial tuning samples.

The SiD Detector, designed for the Future Circular Collider electron-positron collider, has undergone updates in its design, reflecting the SiD Concept Update, and finds additional support from the LEI Detector concept update. The SiD Detector concept aims to provide precise measurements of Higgs and other new physics at an 11-TeV FCC-ee and 100-TeV FCC-hh, and the concept's revisions have been refined by the SiD Collaboration. This document outlines the siD Detector's updates in its detector performance, simulations, and feasibility studies. These updates include enhancements in the detector's ionisation detector, time projection chamber, and calorimeters. We performed the first in-depth analysis of five red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The photometric filter and the missing Ca TRH absorption lines enabled a precise determination of the effective temperatures and metallicities of the stars. We discovered a broad range of [Fe/H] to [Fe/O] mixing in the cluster's stars which contradicts the mass mixing model but supports the mass segregation model. The absorption levels of multiple chemical species in our stellar samples are consistent with each other, supporting the single origin of these stars. The spectroscopic data for our stellar samples show mixing patterns consistent with the mass segregation model rather than the mass mixing model. We found evidence for Ca, Na, and Mg anti-abundance trends in our stellar samples which supports the mass segregation model over the mass mixing model. We determined that Tononzintla 2 has an Mv of 14.03 and an age of approximately 12.5 billion years according to the mass injection model. We found the density core radius of Tononzintla 2 to be 2.3±0.2 pc. We detected a potential metallicity gradient across the cluster which supports the mass segregation model over the mass mixing model. Remote sensing of Earth's surface offers a means to monitor and comprehend environmental changes. The massive datasets generated from remote sensing technologies pose significant processing challenges due to issues like varying resolutions, false colors, and gaps in spatial coverage. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have opened doors for advanced processing of such data using neural networks, despite the inherent limitations posed by Earth-related data. To facilitate the development and deployment of reliable and robust services and applications, a multitude of datasets encompassing Earth-related changes have been compiled and made available to the public. This document delves into the issues associated with accessing these datasets and promotes the incorporation of AI techniques in addressing Earth's problems, while also highlighting the potential benefits for both technical and non-technical stakeholders.

A step-by-step construction method is developed to formulate a simplified dynamical equation for a two-dimensional active nematic's direction, describing its behavior outside of its equilibrium state with minimal reliance on specific microdetails. Utilizing a renaming technique and non-equilibrium renormalization group methods, the newly constructed equation is analyzed, revealing the existence of two distinct phases: an active phase, where some solutions remain linearly stable and others are unstable, and a disorder phase, where all solutions are linearly unstable. During the disorder phase, it's found that some key equations for out-of-equilibrium solitons and other equilibrium structures in active nematics' dynamics possess non-trivial multiplicity, indicating that these structures may be more prevalent than initially thought.

Identifying irregularities in urban data is a pressing research issue. Existing methods primarily focus on identifying irregularities in single-dimensional data and often produce inaccurate detection results when dealing with multi-dimensional data due to the failure to consider the irregularity of neighboring data points. To address these challenges, this paper presents a novel Read approach for recognizing irregularities in regional data on a two-dimensional plane. Read combines the concepts of connectivity and local smoothness to define a partitioning scheme that adapts to different data densities. An empirical evaluation of Read on three real-world datasets reveals that it outperforms three established baseline methods in terms of detection accuracy, while also offering a significantly faster processing speed compared to the HDBSCAN algorithm.

The interaction between two pions is key to understanding the strong force, which in turn affects other aspects of particle physics. The pion vector form factor is essential to this understanding. Many experiments have provided vital data on this form factor. Our study uses two theoretical models to analyze this form factor and predict its behavior at untested energy levels. The dispersion relation method is one such approach we employed. The models' outcomes were compared with experimental data to determine their validity. The price model specifically showed an excellent fit to multiple datasets. With this finding, we used the price model to calculate the pion's contribution to the muon's (g-2) value. The model's results were within the predicted range of the standard model, and its price value aligned with the Fermilab and J-PARC measurements for the hadronic contribution to the recoil effect in (g-2) of the muon.

Developing models from source code necessitates consideration of three key aspects: language syntax, program semantics, and environment semantics. To achieve this, our research aims to create an environment-independent universal representation that accounts for syntactic structure and dynamic behavior. Our proposed model, the Code Universal Representation (CURE), incorporates a novel syntactic encoder and a universal representation learning approach, effectively translating abstract syntax trees into a continuous vector space. Experimentally, CURE demonstrates remarkable performance in predicting Run-Time Behavior (RTB) and identifying code similarities, surpassing leading baselines by over 14% in RB accuracy and 8% in path accuracy while also detecting deeper code relationships beyond surface-level attributes. Furthermore, CURE shows exceptional performance in code security tasks, including vulnerability localization, fault localization, and branch prediction, where our findings consistently outperform baseline models, particularly in RTB prediction and vulnerability localization.

The relation between a galaxy's mass in stars and its surrounding dark matter halo mass has been established for star-forming galaxies by comparing their velocities to their distances from the galactic center. By applying the same method to all galaxies, we reveal a relationship that depends on the morphology of the galaxy, with more elliptical galaxies following the relation more closely. This morphology-dependent relation provides a dynamic basis for previous observations, where early-type galaxies tend to have lighter dark matter halos than similar disk galaxies. Our findings also provide a new way to calibrate the mass relation dynamically, independent of star formation history, and the resulting mass relation agrees with relations derived from more massive galaxies that have had star formation activity.

As an inexpensive and widely available light source, stars serve as reliable indicators for measuring urban air quality without prior data about local dust levels, thanks to its consistent brightness. Our team has been applying photometric aerosel measurements using stellar light for over a decade in metropolitan areas in the UK, with the capability to assess air quality in real-time at any location with a visible light source from stars. Recent advancements in this field have involved integrating these measurements with data from other instruments like the Doppler Lidar and PM10 sensors to improve air quality monitoring and understanding for various applications, including forecasting the impact of low visibility due to specific weather conditions on air travel.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso problems. By extension of the traditional Graphical Lasso model, this framework can incorporate constraints on off-diagonal graph edges using a variety of methods, including convex combinations and weighted $l_1$ penalties. The GGLOasso package is complemented by efficient algorithms, including an iterative thresholding approach and a proximal point method adapted for structured sparsity penalties, both of which demonstrate competitive performance in simulations. It features a Python API with functionality to solve constrained Graphical Lasso problems, estimate geneset associations in genuine data, and visualize the results. We make the GGLOasso package available to support transparent research by providing all code under the MIT open-source license at https://github.com/GGLasso GGLOasso.

We generated theoretical forecasts for the cm-wavelength free-free emission produced by two distinct disk models, tailored to the TW Hydrae young stellar object, and analyzed how photoevaporation affects this phenomenon. According to our analysis, the high-energy photons from the star in this system have a moderate capacity to drive disk photoevaporation. Both disk models predict a flat or slightly inward-sloving emission profile up to approximately 3-4 AU due to high-density contributions. Beyond this radius, the emission slope becomes steeper by 0.3-0.5 in both models as a result of the disk's declining density and temperature. However, the disk evaporation model shows a notable increase in emission between 10 and 30 AU in contrast to both models have marginally increasing free-free emission beyond 30 AU. Both disk models have marginally increasing free-free emission beyond 30 AU. Despite this shared feature, the future detection of emissions from this region of the TW Hydrae's disk would provide evidence for the disk evaporation process.

For speech processing applications, accurately distinguishing between voiced and unvoiced sounds and determining fundamental frequency is crucial. The proposed algorithm leverages a minimum-entropy criterion to make decisions on voiced-unvoiced classification, offering an alternative to traditional methods that rely on heuristics or training data. The speech signal is modelled as a sum of oscillating terms, with the nature of these terms controlled by a sequence of indicators. The indicators are estimated using an optimization process that ensures all oscillating terms are minimized. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through experiments using real speech signals, with the implementation being accessible through an open-source software package.

We introduce a new method, dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward (DWIFOB), to tackle structured monotone inclusion problems. By incorporating the forward-backward algorithm and the extrapolation technique from Anderson acceleration, we develop a globally convergent solution that outperforms existing methods. Furthermore, we provide a globally convergent primal-dual version of DWIFOB and show through numerical tests that it surpasses the performance of the Chambolle-Pock algorithm and the Tikhonov regularized Anderson acceleration, while exhibiting enhanced robustness and reliability.

This research takes place within the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, coupled with a mechanism in its neutral lepton sector in an inverse manner.  By incorporating an inverse mechanism, we can maintain the high level of suppression of lepton number violating effects while achieving non-zero, observable lepton masses.  By including complete stop loop corrections, we can derive the minimal one-loop corrected mass of the lightest CP-higgs boson.  The study also involves direct and indirect constraints on h boson masses from the vacuum stability condition.  By utilizing one-loop corrections in the tree-level condition, we can significantly expand the range of allowed masses for h bosons at various intersection points.  With this data, we can create a prediction for the h boson mass range.  The study also includes one-loop corrections in the neutral scalar sector to correct the mass of the 125 GeV Higgs and investigate the impact on the range of SUSY parameters.  Within this context, we also consider various constraints imposed by experimental data on Higgs boson properties.

The role of neural architecture search (NAS) has escalated within the deep learning community in recent years, however its full potential is hindered by the high computational costs associated with the current search methods. Attempting to tackle this issue, recent research has introduced novel strategies such as exploring subspaces or constructing architectures based on desired properties, yet these approaches often fail to produce optimal results. Attempting to overcome these limitations, this research proposes a new method that combines the benefits of previous techniques, using a property-guided synthesis approach that integrates a property-based neural search space with an exploration of the property space, thus yielding better performance than the state-of-the-art models like the ENR-200 model.

The concept of multicast transmission in millimeter wave (mmWave) networks is being explored to boost network efficiency by transmitting a single signal from the base station (BS) to multiple users simultaneously. However, utilizing digital precoding for this purpose is inefficient due to the need for a full array of antenna elements. A hybrid precoding approach, combining subarrays with multiple digital precifiers, is being investigated as a more suitable solution. This article explores the feasibility of hybrid precoding for multi-group multicasting in mmWave systems through various designs, including those based on semi-definite relaxation (SDR) and codebook search methods. The performance of these designs is evaluated using essential metrics such as the achieved sum-rate and the required number of array elements. Additionally, the results of this study showcase the potential of hybrid precoding arrays in enhancing the system's spectral efficiency.

Federated Learning is a collaborative machine learning approach that preserves data confidentiality by directly involving clients in the training process. It uses a distillation-style learning framework, utilizing a centralized model. To reduce communication costs, several methods have been introduced. We establish a link between Federated Learning and knowledge distillation. Based on this connection, we create a new distillation-based Federated Learning system. We analyze its convergence based on four assumptions. We observe that our proposed method reduces communication complexity when compared to existing techniques. We further introduce two strategies to speed up distillation and significantly decrease round latency. We verify the efficiency of our proposed algorithm through experiments on the CIFAR-100 dataset.

A key feature of Named Data Networking (NDN) is its ability to support future-proof services. Our research centers on service management in NDN-based computing networks, specifically we introduce a service orchestration framework that optimizes the deployment and management of services within such networks. To achieve this, we first outline a marked process to determine the precise location of each service component, with the ultimate goal of minimizing network traffic and ensuring a single data path. We then develop an efficient liveness-checking approach to ensure all services remain operational and interconnected, enabling us to dynamically adjust services without disrupting the network or causing control data overflow. Finally, we utilize service graphs to instantly identify available services and their data paths, ensuring no existing data paths are disrupted, and enabling a fast and seamless network handover during service migrations. Our solution is implemented in the Daedalus network and the OpenWret system, resulting in optimal network traffic reduction, minimal impact on control data, and successful service migrations without disruption.

We tackle the persistent issue of exponential stability for a stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped graph with three equal branches. The outer points where these branches meet are fixed while all other points are free. The graph's central point is strategically positioned, with its distance from the outer points determined by a specific geometric factor related to the radius. This setup mimics the stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped graph but with adjustable branch lengths. The study delves into how stability for these types of beams can be understood by referencing research on the stability of stretched Euler-Bernoulli beams and other similar structures. The authors demonstrate that, under certain conditions, stability is achievable, while in other scenarios, instability is unavoidable. The conclusions drawn from this work are supported by numerical simulations.

In the quark-meson model with a specific type of symmetry breaking, we analyze whether inhomogeneous phases can occur with a specific type of symmetry. With this specific type of symmetry, there is no evidence of symmetry-breaking in the normal phase at a specific temperature threshold, but in the low-temperature phase, there is a possibility of phases where the quarks have no mass, and the matter has spatial patterns, and also a region where the properties are smoothly blended between these patterns and a phase where the quarks have the highest mass.

Utilizing ternary chemical potential phase diagrams and phonon spectrum analysis,
our research shows that compounds $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$ ($M$ = Cd, Hg), derived from Tl$_5$Te$_3$,
exhibit stability in their body-centered tetragonal crystal structure with space group $P4/Nmm$ ($No. 123$).
Our calculations of electronic structure and band structure using the RPMA approach
indicate that $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$ ($M$ = Cd, Hg) are promising candidates for large band gap topological insulators,
with band gaps of approximately $0.162 eV$ and $0.205 eV$, respectively. The analysis of spin-orbit coupling and surface state density confirms the topological insulator nature of these materials. The study also identifies specific values for the $\mathbb{Z}_ 2$ invariant and $Q$ invariant, confirming the occurrence of topological gap states near Fermi level and magnetic moment generation in the presence of perturbations. The investigation of magnetic properties and band structure response to strain and temperature reveals that these materials maintain their topological insulator characteristics under specific conditions. The research indicates that these materials are viable options for creating experiments and topological devices at room temperature.

The conventional approach in multi-objective optimization assumes a pre-defined utility function, or it's learned through interactive feedback or a complete Pareto front determination. However, these methods have limitations as they require the user to specify arbitrary weights, demand extensive interaction with an optimization algorithm, or necessitate full Pareto front discovery. To address these issues, a new utility function learning method is introduced in this paper, where the utility function is learned through a combination of arbitrary initial assumptions and the iterative refinement of the algorithm based on the changes in the utility function's output.

Recent findings in reinforcement learning indicate that agents are susceptible to both white-box and black-box manipulations using adversarial attacks. While previous studies have successfully developed methods for inducing malicious outcomes through adaptive attacks, they typically rely on prior knowledge of the agent or specific system architectures. In contrast, we propose Blackboox, a black-box manipulation technique that relies on the approximate black-box approach, necessitating minimal initial knowledge of the target agent. Through experiments conducted in continuous and semi-Markov environments, we demonstrate that Blackboox can effectively steer an autonomous reinforcement learning agent towards a designated trap region, while competing with state-of-the-art adaptive attack methods in its capacity to induce malicious outcomes.

Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice based on the non-symmorphic wallpaper group pg, which shows linear dispersion in a certain phase. By applying the phase operation, we identify the dirac cones' tunability within the non-symmorphic unit cell, specifically targeting a high-symmetry point. We implement this concept in both a three- and four-atom lattice and calculate the influence of the phase operation on electronic band structures using the non-symmorphic wallpaper group. Additionally, our study reveals the phase operation's effect on effective mass and confirms dirac cones' appearance only for specific phase values. Ultimately, our work provides insight into the impact of non-symmetry on electronic band structures and is relevant to materials like GeS and SnS.

In risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) based on the entropic risk measure, we study an approach for solving non-stationary Markov decision processes (MDPs) in a setting without prior knowledge. The problem is challenging due to the fact that risk-sensitive RL is sensitive to statistical variations, and near-optimal algorithms are difficult to develop when MDP parameters can change over time. We make significant progress in three key areas. First, we introduce a novel loss function that accurately captures the entropic risk measure and rely on it for analysis. Next, we establish a lower bound on the dynamic regret for risk-sensitive RL, and discover that the non-stationary setting is particularly harsh for entropic risk minimization. Finally, we establish the relationship between the exploration-exploitation trade-off and the design of time scales, and achieve nearly optimal bounds for risk-sensitive RL on non-stationary MDPs, in addition to introducing an algorithm for adaptive change detection.

Businesses utilize issue tracking systems to keep an eye on their projects' progress.
The data generated by these systems offers valuable insights into a company's operational efficiency.
To gain access to these records, researchers have generally relied on historical data from publicly available sources.
However, these sources are typically outdated and lack current representations of issue tracking systems.
To address this limitation, we developed and released a collection of publicly accessible Jiras.
These Jiras provide up-to-date data on Jira's interface, functionalities, customization options, security measures, and usage patterns.
Our dataset encompasses the activities of 283,159 unique users and facilitates the investigation of 653,541 interconnections, including collaborations, communications, resource allocations, and dependencies.
We have also identified and discussed several unique characteristics of the Jira platform.
To support future studies, we have explored different research inquiries and suggested possible research questions.

Decentralized machine learning applications such as autonomous driving and drone operation could benefit from distributed machine learning (DML) over device graphs. The typical approach to aggregation in DML is averaging, which is used in algorithms like Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). However, averaging can introduce a non-negligible bias in the model updates, especially over complex network topologies and with heterogeneous data distributions. This has a considerable impact on the model's convergence speed and final accuracy. This research introduces a new class of aggregation functions tailored for model averaging that reduces this DML bias. The proposed functions significantly enhance convergence and accuracy over the standard averaging method. The innovation lies in the properties of these functions, which ensure a balanced aggregation of gradients regardless of the network topology or data distribution. The authors formulate an optimization problem to determine the aggregation functions, applying a dual problem transformation. The results show that the novel aggregation functions can improve the model's accuracy and efficiency in DML applications.

A monolithically integrated multi-grating system has been proposed to establish a connection between isolated atoms and photonic chip technology, enabling the precise direction and convergence of lasers towards the chip surface to capture, manipulate and detect single Rubidium atoms. This includes an optical dipole trap formed by the intersection of two laser beams of 850 nm, creating a pattern of traps with diameters of around 2.7 micrometers per atom, which guides a probe laser of 780 nm to stimulate and collect fluorescence emitted by the atoms. This design offers the possibility to utilize smaller atoms, yielding tighter confinement capabilities. This proposed architecture has the potential to be utilized in a range of applications including the development of single-atom lasers, quantum registers for integrated photonic quantum computing, and high-sensitivity sensors based on single atoms.

Let the monoid of finite words, denoted $\Lambda^{\ast}$, be defined over an alphabet $\Lambda$ with a possible order. The preorder on this monoid results from the underlying alphabetical order and its Cartesian product. The completion of this monoid in the continuous, complete lattice of preorder ideals is known as the MacNeille completion. In the case where the alphabetical order is comparable, the MacNeille completion of this monoid is completed in the case of a strict order. This completion can be characterized both topologically and syntactically. While the topological characterization is based on specific topological properties, the syntactic characterization is based on the properties of ranked, well-formed and minimally ambiguous grammars in order for the language of this grammar to represent the macneille completion of this monoid.

A recent study addressed a crucial problem in rational polymer design by employing a method to predict polymer properties based on monomer level data and linear regression. The outcome provided optimal target values for unspecified properties and corresponding optimal monomers needed to achieve these goals. The study further explored the effects of swapping these monomers while maintaining the target values. Nevertheless, the study limited itself to polycrystalline, and not stochastically coiled, polymers despite this being a significant type of polymer. The objective became achieving the same design criteria while replacing the linear dependence on monomers with nonlinear alternatives suitable for modeling this polymer type. This goal was realized by reformulating the problem using mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) and solving it using specific solvers. The resulting work presented a method utilizing nonlinear alternatives to achieve the same design criteria as before. The study utilized the PyMOPAL software library to demonstrate the approach with various inflexible and flexible target values, and the results showed that the swap ranges narrowed significantly when the original problem was replaced with its nonlinear version. The study further compared two different optimization techniques in achieving these goals and the findings showed substantial differences in outcome with notable variations in swap ranges. The study specifically highlighted the importance of considering discrete amounts of monomers when designing polymers and the limitations of linear programming in accurately predicting polymer properties. The study concluded with suggestions on further improvements in rational polymer design.

This paper presents a straightforward approach to solving complex optimization problems over time. Tradifying continuous problems into discrete ones allows the use of nonlinear regression techniques for finding solutions. We've chosen direct transcription methods due to their versatility and ease of implementation, specifically collocation, as illustrated through a case study on adjusting ventilator settings. We've explored the challenges of ventilation, focusing on the simultaneous treatment of two COVID-19 patients and the compromises required to achieve optimal outcomes.

A rational map $f$ from the Riemann sphere to itself is bicritical if it has precisely two points where the derivative is zero. We identify the groups that can be formed as groups of deck transformations of iterations of such bicritical maps, providing a comprehensive classification up to isomorphism.

In the context of high-dimensional linear regression, our analysis centers on the Bayesian approach using data-driven priors derived from [1]. Notably, these priors exhibit beneficial posterior contraction characteristics and efficient computational performance. Building upon this foundation, our research expands on the existing theoretical frameworks by accommodating the scenario of unknown error variance under a sparsity assumption, ultimately demonstrating model selection consistency, optimal contraction rates, and satisfying the conditions of the Bernstein von Mises theorem via a multivariate t-distribution analysis.

To address the critical issue of high energy consumption and its associated costs and environmental impact in machining processes, this research paper suggests utilizing Bayesian cost analysis and the GenCo package in R for Bayesian computational costs to optimize specific parameters such as feed rate, withdrawal, and cutting depth to minimize energy expenses. The genetic algorithm-based optimization method provided by the GenCo package enables the precise determination of optimal values for these parameters to reduce energy costs. The study compares analytical and computational approaches to energy costs and explores the correlations between energy consumption and other cost metrics like tooling costs and surface finish quality. Ultimately, the study seeks to find the optimal balance between these costs to achieve efficient and cost-effective energy management in machining processes.

The spectral dimension of a weighted graph is an exponent that describes the random walk's behavior on the graph, whereas the Ahlfors-regular conformal dimension of the graph's distance is an invariant characteristic. We present a counterexample disproving a previously held inequality concerning these dimensions, particularly for fractals lacking scale symmetry, as well as establish a condition under which the inequality holds in scale-symmetric graphs.

Utilizing the principles of $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing, we introduce an innovative method to isolate the physical properties of the hadronic $Y(4230)$ resonance from existing experimental data. Experimenters have previously identified multiple possible solutions through the analysis of its decay products. Employing our novel approach, we successfully select a singular, physically relevant solution out of the myriad options presented. We identify the resonance $Y(4230)$ as a $1^{--}$ state and determine its mass and total width to be 4230 MeV and 361 MeV, respectively. Furthermore, we calculate the branching fractions for the radiative decays $Y(4230) \to J/\psi \gamma$ and $Y(4230) \to \psi(2S) \gamma$ to be 3.49e-03 and 6.98e-03, respectively. These computed values can guide forthcoming experimental investigations.

This research introduces three indices for online signature templates that measure distinctiveness, complexity, and uniqueness. Distinctiveness index evaluates the model's capability to differentiate between genuine and impostor signature attempts, with higher values indicating better performance. Complexity index reflects the relative difficulty of online signature maneuvers between different users, with higher values indicating more complex signatures. Uniqueness index assesses the model's ability to capture variations within the same user's different signature attempts, with higher values reflecting greater uniqueness. Empirical validation using the signature database demonstrated the proposed indices' effectiveness in evaluating these critical aspects.

We investigated four-point amplitude calculations in the most fundamental string theory examples featuring T-fold backgrounds with six supersymmetries in four dimensions. These theories are represented as asymmetric orbifolds of the fundamental M-theory framework. Our findings demonstrate that in the lowest-order perturbative analysis, higher-derivative corrections are consistent with a supergravity theory that includes a specific coupling structure, confirming a previous hypothesis put forth by [A. Klemm, A. Reys, and T. Wrase, arXiv:1812.01653]. We discovered inconsistencies in the leading-order perturbative analysis that would necessitate the introduction of unphysical states or violate the expected helicity selection rules. Additionally, we explored the possibility of non-perturbative corrections overcoming these challenges, which could potentially resolve these issues.

Theoretical investigations have employed higher-order correlation functions as a crucial tool to examine complex systems in quantum simulators, particularly quantum gas microscopes. Researchers have leveraged the measurements of specific correlations in the two-dimensional Hubbard model with hole doped from an insulating antiferromagnetic state. Our calculations leverage fluctuation concepts to determine correlation functions and examine the effects of a single hole on surrounding spin and spin-wave excitations. We observe the coexistence of multiple hole behaviors, including the hole being trapped by the hole and the hole being free to move due to kinetic effects. By analyzing our results through the order in which they are calculated, we uncover crucial insights into how spins align in the vicinity of the hole's location.

We examined the global spread of nitrogen-to-oxygen ratios in galactic super-novae remnants to infer the nucleosynthetic processes within stars. By analyzing the nitrogen contents, we addressed the long-standing query regarding the origin of significant amounts of nitrogen. Our results from four galactic SNRs show varying N/O ratios, and we deduced the mass ranges and stellar evolution processes of intermediate-mass stars (8-40 solar masses) under different metallicity conditions. Furthermore, we explored the proportion of nitrogen produced by massive low-metallicity stars versus massive stars with higher metallicities. Our findings are consistent with previous studies, and we derived a constraint on the yield of intermediate-mass stars producing around 0.025 solar masses.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, particularly in instances where one language functions as a secondary language, and a primary language is not sufficient for expressing complex ideas. This phenomenon is more prevalent in certain multilingual societies than others, particularly where a primary language lacks a written form. Individual language preferences also play a significant role in code-mixing patterns. For instance, Hindu users in India frequently combine code-mixes of English with Devanagari-based languages like Hindi and Sanskrit. This study examines the NLP challenges associated with analyzing code-mixed content and highlights essential considerations for developing NLP systems to support such users in diverse social settings.

Biomedical networks serve as a fundamental tool for understanding interconnected entities and their relationships, which are widely used in modeling various biomedical networks, such as drug-target networks, and disease associations. The rapid accumulation of data across multiple domains makes it essential to extract relevant information efficiently. This chapter focuses on the importance of graph representation learning in the biomedicine field, discussing its applications in tasks like predicting novel drug targets and interactions, as well as non-binary disease associations. The chapter also highlights future research directions in biomedical graph representation learning.

Weakly Interacting Massive Particles can be trapped in compact stars, such as white dwarves, resulting in an increase in gamma-ray emission from these stars. A novel analysis of the recoil spectrum caused by P M1-TRAPPIST-1 reveals that models featuring an SU(2)_L x U(1)_Y x U(1)_{W'} left-right symmetric model with specific properties may explain the observed excess in radiation from certain stars near PA-2019 BCG. This scenario proposes that W_R dark matter particles interact via a heavy particle that decays into standard model particles within the star's environment. However, further research involving more precise white dwarf data may refute this model's validity.

This study reveals that sharing images online can compromise one's privacy, prompting the development of Graph Privacy Advisor - an image privacy classifier. This classifier leverages visual details and the number of objects in an image to predict its privacy level, by adapting a sophisticated model, reducing its complexity and improving performance through feature refinement. In particular, the classifier identifies the most relevant image characteristics to use for privacy evaluation and substitutes complex, high-dimensional image data with simplified features, thus reducing its complexity. Moreover, the classifier tackles the issue of preconceived biases by modeling the likelihood of objects appearing together, rather than the frequency of individual objects within each class.

Building on Griffiths' model of a quantum radiator, I expand upon it by developing theoretical models that can represent high entropy levels in isolated quantum systems. These models are constrained to adhere to the principles of unitary evolution, reflecting the idea that information is preserved within closed quantum systems. The radiative processes in these models are designed such that intermediate stages expose substantial amounts of data, yet the system's final state is marked by complete purity, confirming the initial conditions. In order to test the efficacy of the radiative process in revealing underlying system information, I introduce a quantitative indicator known as the entropic emission measure, which estimates how much data is released during the process. I utilize this indicator to evaluate the efficacy of the models in exposing system information and to compare the efficacy of different observables used in the process of measurement. I also introduce additional models incorporating multiple degrees of freedom in the emitted particles, such as mass variations, and demonstrate that our choices of indicators can be adjusted to reflect differences in the availability of different types of information.

Measurements of charged-particle fragmentation in proton-proton and lead-lead collisions at the LHC are carried out with the ATLAS detector, examining the difference between the two interaction types and the gluon's role in the fragmentation function in proton-proton collisions. The fragmentation functions in proton-proton collisions are measured using jet algorithm, variable width chebyshev polynomials, and the relative difference between the two interaction types is analyzed by comparing the fragmentation functions in lead-lead and proton-proton collisions. The results are consistent with predictions across the examined range of scaled fragmentation functions.

The CP2K program package, often seen as an indispensable tool in atomistic simulations, highlights its capabilities particularly in carrying out ab-initio molecular dynamics through the application of the Car-Parrinello method's latest advancements. It then delves into current developments in low-scaling, massively parallel eigenvalue solvers and post-Hartree-Fock computations. The presentation also outlines innovative strategies for leveraging future low-precision computing architectures to the fullest potential. Our strategy here involves pairing the submatrix approach with approximate computing techniques to effectively address the demands of the impending exascale era.

Small solar eruptions known as nanoflares may hold the key to explaining the solar corona's high temperatures through a process of self-heating, according to the flare-related coronal heating theory. Furthermore, nanoflares are believed to amplify the correlation between coronal and foreshock X-ray emissions during microflares. We present data from the Flare Onboard X-ray Spectroscopic Imager (FOXSI) instrument, a component of the Rastering X-ray Imager (RXI) payload, that observed a minor solar eruption on April 11th of 2019. The eruption initially produced white-light sigs, followed by the observation of its coronal and foreshock X-ray emissions for approximately 200 seconds. The X-ray emissions from both the coronal and foreshock regions were detected with energy levels above 20 keV. Notably, the Coronal X-rays had fluxes as low as 3.5E-4 and 5.0E-4 times 10^-4 W/m^2, respectively. The observed coronal X-ray emission intensity was lower than expected based on typical scaling laws. The intensity of the foreshock X-ray emission was used to estimate the solar eruption's peak rate, which turned out to be on the lower end of what is usually observed in nanoflares. In machine learning, particularly in natural language processing and computer vision, data augmentation has been used to enhance model performance. Despite its success, there has been a lack of research on applying this technique to graph neural networks. This study aims to address this gap by developing a method that combines train- and test-time augmentation to improve social influence prediction. Utilizing a variational graph autoencoder in both phases allows for the generation of multiple augmented social network graphs. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate that this end-to-end approach outperforms existing baseline models, showcasing the efficacy of augmentation on graph neural networks for social influence prediction. This finding is significant as it opens up new avenues for conducting more accurate social influence predictions in real-world scenarios.

Quantum field theory complexity is a challenging concept to define, and our work provides concrete predictions for it within conformal field theories. We establish that the time-dependent complexity of a state, measured by the KV-magnetization, grows linearly over time at a rate proportional to λ times the overlap between the state and the primary operator. Rate values below or above one indicate the presence of or absence of entangled subsystems, respectively. We validate these findings through numerical simulations of the Ising model at its critical point across different lattices. The rate value of 0.46 is obtained with a high degree of precision, and we observe that increasing the system size leads to greater accuracy.

This theoretical work offers a comprehensive framework for the task of estimating object pose from total least squares, where features from the object are aligned with features in its surrounding environment. Not only do we define and define the optimality criteria for this alignment, but we also present a solution that guarantees a unique and optimal result, regardless of the level of noise or measurement inaccuracies in the features' coordinates. Additionally, we show that our framework can effectively handle partial overlaps of the object with its visible features. Furthermore, our algorithm demonstrates resilience to objects with symmetry and the presence of outliers, all of which are significant considerations in real-world applications. Finally, our analysis is not confined to two-dimensional surfaces but applies equally to three-dimensional objects, as long as the volume data is available.

This note examines the possibility that in models of supergravity and string theory, sectors which influence the superpotential and those that determine the kinetic terms for moduli may have different temperatures. We demonstrate the implications this has on the mechanism of moduli stabilization, particularly when considering the Seiberg duality for field theories described by supersymmetric QCD. We also explore moduli stabilization within a supersymmetric $SU(N)$ gauge theory with $N+1$ chiral superfields, showing that an anti-de Sitter vacuum can emerge if the theory's kinetic terms follow specific geometric structures. We provide examples of such constraints in strings of type I and orientifolds, as well as in supergravity theories with specific superpotentials, opening the door for the development of duality arguments in string theory and supergravity that could lead to de Sitter vacua.

Researchers have discovered an instance of same-sign W boson pair production in proton-proton collisions. The study utilized data gathered at a high-energy proton collider, specifically 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ worth of data, collected at a 13 TeV energy setting with a sophisticated particle detector. The observation process focused on distinctive patterns of charged and neutral leptons, accompanied by jettiness in the event, which align with theoretical predictions of certain Standard Model interactions. The study's findings show that these patterns match expectations based on the combination of direct top quark decay processes and rare charged current neutral current events. The study's data accurately correspond with the foreseen outcomes of theoretical models.

This study investigates the capabilities of color enhancement models in expanding their training data by processing grayscale images from unknown cameras. Our research addresses the challenges associated with domain shift in color enhancement, specifically through changes in camera systems. Our hypothesis is that existing reference images can be utilized to adapt the architecture of color enhancement models when a new camera system is introduced. Consequently, this technique could improve the diversity and coverage of datasets for camera-specific changes. However, we approach this problem from a different perspective, proposing that deep camera conversion models can adapt across different camera systems without relying on reference images. This proposal constitutes a multi-camera color enhancement problem. We evaluate various combinations of datasets and technologies to determine their effects on camera-specific changes. Our findings reveal that incorporating images from multiple devices yields noticeable improvements in performance. In particular, integrating high-resolution images has been shown to have a significant impact on the quality of generated colors.

We examined the performance of six cosmological models by analyzing data from the Planck satellite, incorporating lensing information from CMB radiation. Focusing on the models $\Lambda$CDM, DS$\Lambda$CDM, CDM, DCM, DECDM, and $\Lambda$CDM2, with a time-variable equation-of-state parameter for a second cosmological fluid in the latter two models, we determined their hierarchical relationships using the Bayesian model selection method. Our analysis revealed that the data were most consistent with the models $\Lambda$CDM2 and $\Lambda$CDM, with a preferred Hubble constant of around 67.25 ± 0.42 km/s/Mpc. Additionally, a model involving a single fluid with an equation-of-state parameter consistent with a cosmological constant performed poorly compared to its two-component counterpart. To gain further insight, we analyzed the consistency of these models with two independent datasets of BAO and SHOES, with a focus on their joint fit to the standard CD$\Lambda$M model. Our results indicated a significant tension at approximately 2.4$\sigma$ between the model's predicted and observed values of the lensing potential amplitude.

The advent of online collaboration tools like GitHub has made it easy for software developers to share and reuse code across various repositories. The process of adapting existing code from one repository to another, known as maintenance, has become a areas of focus within the development community. We investigated this phenomenon on a larger scale using the concept of "maintenance" to analyze the entire codebase on the GitHub platform. A approach was developed to track changes in files that are the same in multiple repositories, allowing a more comprehensive understanding of how developers utilize and modify shared code. The approach was evaluated using a large dataset of open-source projects and revealed that developers are actively using repositories for more than just their original purpose. The findings also highlighted important insights into how developers use and modify code in these repositories.

The 2013 TESS mission discovered an exciting Tyc 5611.4432 eclipsing binary with potential properties of a gamma Doradus variable star, which has a well-established amplitude of variation exceeding 10 parts per million through photometric data. Notably, these data also reveal a significantly smaller secondary eclipse amplitude, corresponding to less than one percent of the primary eclipse amplitude, along with an intriguing data anomaly.  Further data analysis shows that the system's rate of mass loss may cause the shifting of spectral lines due to the Doppler effect, causing the red side to shift in one direction and the blue side to shift in the opposite direction.  A forthcoming study will utilize TESS data along with spectroscopic data to further investigate this system with a larger dataset and determine its true nature.

This paper builds upon previous work of the second author with Daskalopoulos and Vazquez, which involved introducing a Yamabe flow based on fractional curvature and demonstrating the existence of mild solutions. The current research expands on that study by establishing the convergence of the flow under certain data conditions within a broader framework.

Cross-domain recommendation has emerged as a promising approach for resolving the issue of severe data scarcity in niche categories. Current methods successfully leverage shared preferences across domains but fail to consider the diverse representation of different domains in notable ways. To address this limitation, we introduce MSDCR, a novel method that not only harnesses shared user and item preferences but also exploits multiple distinct domain representations to capture domain-specific characteristics. To enhance comprehensive aspect-based learning in separate domains, MSDCR incorporates a dual mechanism: employing distinct attention mechanisms to identify key features within each domain and a multi-domain contrastive learning module that minimizes intra-domain similarity and encourages inter-domain heterogeneity. Experimentally, MSDCR achieved superior results over competing approaches in handling small child categories and demonstrated the robustness of its comprehensive aspect preference learning mechanism.

We establish that the deformation space of a sheaf over a smooth projective variety is defined by the first hypercohomology of a constructed complex for orthogonal and symplectic cases. Additionally, our study introduces an obstruction theory, which targets the second hypercohomology space.

Andrews and Merca's findings on even partitions with distinct parts, quantified by A000009, are extended here. The analysis now includes a specific constraint: elements of the partition cannot exceed size two. The findings are generalized further, with findings presented for partitions with limited parts of size at most two, and specifically, those limited to sizes two and three.

Given n randomly drawn samples of a complex-valued function, f, from a domain D, under a measure mu, we investigate the theoretical $L_2$ approximation error. We establish that with higher sample sizes, $L_2$ estimates converge at a specific rate and with fewer samples convergence is statistically assured. Notably, we avoid assuming specific properties of the function, function smoothness, or data uniform distribution. We demonstrate the practical application of our findings on various data sets, including data from numerical simulations and real-world observations, without measurement noise. We also develop a procedure for estimating the $L_2$ error of a function within finite-dimensional subspaces of Hilbert spaces.

To investigate the transportation and yield production of the $J/\psi$, $\psi(2S)$, $B_c$ and X(3872) in heavy-ion collisions, a kinetic-rate equation is employed and compared with data from the RHIC and LHC experiments. The study focuses on how these particles' relative yields are affected by initial conditions, such as their abundance in a thermal state, during the process of high-energy nuclear collisions. In particular, research into kinetic equilibrium reveals that in central collisions, the $J/\psi$ yield matches the experimental observation at RHIC energy levels above 20 GeV, while discrepancies exist at lower energies. The study also indicates that incorporating regeneration effects explains $J/\psi$ overproduction at certain LHC experiments, specifically the RHIC-BREMS experiment, and predicts a specific $J/\psi$ yield that may be verified in near-future RHIC runs. The research predicts a very low $B_c$ yield in high-energy kinetic collisions, especially for smaller nuclei like AuAu and PbPb. However, $B$-meson abundance is accurately predicted. The study found that $\psi(2S)$ has a suppressed abundance compared to $J/\psi$ that is lower than initially expected from kinetic analysis. The study did however discover that $\psi(2S)$ is more abundant than $J/\psi$ in certain high-energy Au+Au RHIC experiments. The study predicted that $J/\psi

The occurrence of local moments is widespread in disordered semiconductor materials, such as silicon doped with boron, and it is seen more frequently when these materials are near a metal's transition point. Researchers have found that local moments can also be found in theoretical models of disordered interacting chains, such as the 1D disordered Schrieffer-Wolf-Lockett model and the 1D disordered Kondo model, which are considered special cases of the Hubbard model. However, the theoretical understanding of how local moments arise in the most general form of the Hubbard model has been limited. This has led to the creation of a new mean-field model based on the Hubbard model that shows the system can transition between an RS phase and a delocalized phase depending on the level of disorder. This new model also demonstrates that the transition between these two systems is a higher-order transition.

The entries are determined by the group's G generators, which are denoted as (s_1,s_2,...,s_n). The order of these generators is specified by a Coxeter graph, which defines the order of the group's elements and thus its G generators.
